This is a remarkably bad book.

Here is the opening of The Hacienda:

THE LOW SWEEP OF the southern horizon was a perfect line, unmarred by even the smudge of horses tossing their heads in the distance. The road yawned empty.

The carriage was gone.

I stood with my back to the gates of Hacienda San Isidro. Behind me, high white stucco walls rose like the bones of a long-dead beast jutting from dark, cracked earth. Beyond the walls, beyond the main house and the freshly dug graves behind the capilla, the tlachiqueros took their machetes to the sharp fields of maguey. Wandering the fields as a boy taught me agave flesh does not give like man’s; the tlachiqueros lift their machetes and bring them down again, and again, each dull thud seeking the heart’s sweet sap, each man becoming more intimately acquainted with the give of meat beneath metal, with the harvesting of hearts.

A breeze snaked into the valley from the dark hills, its dry chill stinging my cheeks and the wet in my eyes. It was time to turn back. To return to my life as it was. Yet the idea of turning, of gazing up at San Isidro’s heavy wooden doors alone, slicked my palms with sweat.

There was a reason I had once set my jaw and crossed San Isidro’s threshold, a reason why I passed through its gates like a reckless youth from legends of journeys to the underworlds.

That reason was gone.

And still I stood in the center of the dirt road that led away from San Isidro, away from Apan, my eyes fixed on the horizon with the fervor of a sinner before their saint. As if the force of my grief alone could transcend the will of God and return that carriage. Return the woman who had been taken from me. The echo of retreating hoofbeats and the clouds of dust they left curled in the air like copal incense, mocking me.

Here is the opening of Rebecca:

Last night I dreamed I went to Manderley again. It seemed to me I stood by the iron gate leading to the drive, and for a while I could not enter, for the way was barred to me. There was a padlock and a chain upon the gate. I called in my dream to the lodge keeper, and had no answer, and peering closer through the rusted spokes of the gate I saw that the lodge was uninhabited.

No smoke came from the chimney, and the little lattice windows gaped forlorn. Then, like all dreamers, I was possessed of a sudden with supernatural powers and passed like a spirit through the barrier before me. The drive wound away in front of me, twisting and turning as it had always done, but as I advanced I was aware that a change had come upon it; it was narrow and unkept, not the drive that we had known. At first I was puzzled and did not understand, and it was only when I bent my head to avoid the low swinging branch of a tree that I realized what had happened. Nature had come into her own again and, little by little, in her stealthy, insidious way had encroached upon the drive with long, tenacious fingers. The woods, always a menace even in the past, had triumphed in the end. They crowded, dark and uncontrolled, to the borders of the drive. The beeches with white, naked limbs leaned close to one another, their branches intermingled in a strange embrace, making a vault above my head like the archway of a church. And there were other trees as well, trees that I did not recognize, squat oaks and tortured elms that straggled cheek by jowl with the beeches, and had thrust themselves out of the quiet earth, along with monster shrubs and plants, none of which I remembered.

The drive was a ribbon now, a thread of its former self, with gravel surface gone, and choked with grass and moss. The trees had thrown out low branches, making an impediment to progress; the gnarled roots looked like skeleton claws. Scattered here and again among this jungle growth I would recognize shrubs that had been landmarks in our time, things of culture and grace, hydrangeas whose blue heads had been famous. No hand had checked their progress, and they had gone native now, rearing to monster height without a bloom, black and ugly as the nameless parasites that grew beside them.

Rebecca immediately establishes the anxieties, mysteries, and setting that will preoccupy the narrative. The Hacienda establishes that paragraph breaks can be used to create a cheap sense of drama. The Hacienda also opens with a flashback, by the way, and if you're thinking "well perhaps we will be shown important things that happened in the past", let me assure you: we will not.

Harping on comps feels a little cheap but here I think it's very relevant, because when you comp Rebecca in your marketing you will in fact be faced with the expectations of people who liked Rebecca. You're setting your author up for failure the same way Warner Bros would set a director up for failure by purchasing a Barney remake and advertising it as a Jurassic Park sequel. There's nothing wrong with remaking Barney but the people who came to the theater for Jurassic Park are going to be annoyed. Don't worry about feeling too bad for the author, though, because this book is an incoherent mess of her own doing.

Our protagonist Beatriz's father is dead and she hates living with her aunt, so she marries the owner of an hacienda and goes to live there. The house is haunted, the guy might've killed his first wife, and there's a priest who is a boywitch. Fun! Over the course of the book they banish the ghost, find the real murderer, & Beatriz gets repeatedly told by every single darker-skinned poorer person around her that she's not like the other wife, she's special, and better.

The prose is very bad on a technical level. It is repetitive in vocabulary and structure and fails to sustain any sense of atmosphere or mood.

I don't have much to say about the plot except it is boring and poorly executed. We are repeatedly informed that the house is evil, the heroine sees red eyes in the corner, etc, but each nasty little supernatural incident is a bastion of telling-not-showing. By the halfway point of the book, we already basically understand the nature of the haunting, but we are subjected to hundreds more pages of people running around and dealing with the logistics of the haunting. It is boring.

Gender-wise, this book hates women!

Beatriz is mestiza and married money (Rodolfo) so that she could escape from a life of drudgery as the indigent relation of her mother's family. As the book progresses, she comes to realize that becoming a plantation mistress because you wanted independence is ethically sketchy regardless of how mean your aunt is. Unfortunately her end conclusion is "haciendas are fine if the right people are in charge of them, and also I personally should have married for love and stayed close to my mother".

Beatriz likes to mouth off to crucifixes and befriend servants, but she has very few traits beyond "as the daughter of a general I refuse". The author famously said she wanted to write a protagonist with more agency than a typical gothic novel, and in this she comprehensively failed. Beatriz screams, falls down, and follows her servants around going "tell me I'm good tell me I'm good". Calling her an empty vessel would be an insult to bowls. Calling her a ventriloquist's dummy would be an insult to Jim Henson. She is an avatar of the author's anxiety whose inner life the author is palpably bored by.

Beatriz is surrounded by other women who exist either to be evil or to tell her she's not like other girls. The boywitch's cousin, Paloma, is a servant in the hacienda. She is dark-skinned, quiet, and literate. She reinforces that Beatriz isn't like the first wife; at the end of the book, Beatriz rewards her for her loyalty and good-heartedness by making her the "heir to the foreman" of the hacienda. Remember, kids: work hard and suck up to the right people and you, too, can be handed a whip with which to beat your relatives.

Rodolfo's sister, Juana, is a bastard who kills Rodolfo and Doña Catalina. She exists on the page as a half-hearted red herring and then a one-dimensional villain. Juana is a cruel racist and yet still has a higher villain kill count than Beatriz. This is annoying. Also annoying is that she is basically a homophobic stereotype of an "independent woman" who isn't even an on-page dyke.

We only meet Doña Catalina in apparitions and flashbacks. She is a classic Evil Bitch: blonde, cruel, racist, murderous. But she also, in one of the worst scenes of the book, spots the boywitch with his cousin and immediately deduces that he was making an abortion brew. Allow me to suggest that if you recognize an abortion recipe by firelight, you are yourself an abortionist. This incoherence of plot and POV are emblematic of the book.

SPEAKING OF THE BOYWITCH! THERE IS SO MUCH GENDER GOING ON WITH THE BOYWITCH! The boywitch, whose name is Andrés, was raised in the tradition by his grandmother. He has a fractured understanding of his witchy heritage and his witchcraft is narratively and spiritually incoherent, which we will get to, but I want to note that his magic is fundamentally gender-neutral in a way that is not true to history nor the otherwise heavily gendered division of labor within the book. He does everything: abortions, treating illness, calling rain, etc. He is surrounded by women who covet his gift and beg him to use it for them. He is the other POV character, though Beatriz has more time on the page, and his POV is transparently the one the author is actually interested in. His perspective closes the novel; he's the one who actually banishes the ghost after the heroine gets tied up, cries, and runs away. My note regarding his position in the narrative: "the most gothic thing about this book is the torturous difference between what the author wants to be writing (normie reylo-adjacent het romance with a male lead) and what she is actually writing (ostensibly feminist dual-POV ghost story)."

The hacienda is haunted by a ghost yet has its own sentience. This magic is primarily experienced by Beatriz but accessed by Andrés. In addition to being a boywitch, Andrés does exorcisms in the Catholic tradition and also has a "box of darkness" that he can't/won't access until the book's finale. "Box of darkness" is in quotes because the darkness is described as both literal darkness locked inside a physical box which is hidden, and also, metaphorical darkness that lives in André's chest and which he represses for safety.

I think the author thinks she's doing something with loss of heritage, colonization, etc. in how she portrays Andrés' magic. Unfortunately the writing is not good. Andrés is a priest who cannot decide if he is a full-on atheist, a Catholic with non-Catholic heritage, or a committed Catholic, and the narrative only bothers to portray the Catholic parts of his background with precision or specificity. His grandmother's language is breathlessly described by Beatriz as "silky, sinuous". His rituals are half-remembered to the point of genericization: "witch's glyphs" and "exorcism glyphs" are casually mentioned, and the difference between them, in faith tradition or power or physical construction, is elided. On top of the mixture of Catholic and indigenous practice (which does have its root in history and current practice), Andrés has dangerous, instinctual power that he calls "the darkness". Again: this is literal darkness in a literal box and also metaphorical darkness. Its primary purpose in the narrative is serving as a deus ex machina. But Andrés' grandmother knew about "the darkness" and impressed upon Andrés that he had to figure out how to manage his own individual power. The idea of witchcraft as individualistic power is reinforced throughout the narrative. Because this idea is articulated through the lens of a colonized priest, it largely serves to reify the authority of the Catholic church while treating all other faith traditions as, to use the language of my people, syntactic sugar. The overall effect is one of Christian supremacism. All other faith traditions are murky, dark, ill-defined and unintelligible. Christianity is precise and essential to banishing the ghost.

Ambiguous magic is fine and can enhance a narrative. But in an historical fantasy novel, I expect the author to understand how her magic works and to be aware of how Christianity can derail all other traditions you seek to depict. This book repeatedly reinforces the systems it wants to undermine. To avoid this fate the author would have needed to spend more time on Andrés' personal history and less time on the erotics of staring at a boywitch-priest.

In addition to the rank & dank implications of "witchcraft is spooky mumbo-jumbo, the rosary is pure and simple", the book all but refuses to engage in the violence of the hacienda system or what it would mean to people living there. The author states that she researched haciendas extensively, and based on the included details I believe that. However, having your characters say that the hacienda is bad and caste systems are bad is not the same thing as structuring your narrative around this understanding.

Beatriz and Andrés have different relationships to the hacienda. To Beatriz, it starts as a symbol of independence and ends as a burden. To Andrés, it is a site of familial attachment and also pain. And that is where things get weird.

Throughout the narrative, Andrés conflates hacienda-as-building and hacienda-as-land. He repeatedly articulates an attachment to the land and a fear of the land's owners, yet he is strikingly attached to the trappings of their ownership. He states that he's "the witch of the valley", that he has a responsibility to care for the villagers, etc, and he also shows Beatriz that his family is buried in shit tier plots in the corner of the hacienda's cemetery. His family has been on the land for at least as long as the hacienda existed (seven generations). His family has been harmed by the hacienda's owners, the Solórzanos, for at least that long. His cousin was raped and murdered by the Solórzanos. He himself was banished from the land by the Solórzanos.

At the end of the book, after Doña Catalina's ghost has been banished, he returns to the hacienda and the house is gently teasing to him. It is explicitly described as sentient and childlike in its innocence. You know, the great house, where all his ancestors were raped and murdered and borderline enslaved. It's a nice place, once the single malevolent spirit is dealt with.

This is a catastrophic failure of narration, but I wasn't particularly surprised to see it, because Andrés' return to the hacienda is preceded by Beatriz leaving. In her leavetaking, she works with Paloma to develop a business plan for the hacienda, reopen the hacienda's general store, and set Paloma up to be foreman of the hacienda long-term. The author says "systems of power are bad" and the story says "unless the right people are in charge, in which case, they're fine!"

I come from the Southeast US and I am very familiar with the style of social justice that can't stop saying "but the architecture really was beautiful". It is unconscionable to put this stuff in a book in 2022. If you want to write a poltergeist story, that is your lookout, but I am struggling to understand how a man whose ancestors were literally raped and murdered inside a sentient structure can stand inside that structure and be like "wow now that the ghost is gone I love this house so much". I'm sure this narrative tension could be dealt with, but to do so, you'd have to acknowledge the existence of that tension. The author does not do this.

Additionally, the narrative repeatedly tells us about the "land": the importance of it to everyone in the story, its power to grant independence, etc. Unfortunately the land is barely described. There is maguey, we are told. Juana gets darker-skinned by traipsing around the fields all day. Andrés' family was on the land before the Spaniards were, but he has no real opinion about it. We aren't told anything about the land except that it exists: not how it changed, not how it is cultivated, not its geography or climate. The narrative of place is entirely invested in the house itself. This makes Andrés' pathos fall flat at best. At worse, he seems like a hypocrite who doesn't care that he's standing on floors soaked with the blood of his own ancestors.

Finally: ghost stories and gothic narratives are not the same thing, and this book doesn't understand the distinction, very much to its detriment.

Ghost stories and gothic novels do, of course, overlap significantly. You'll find ghosts all over gothic novels, and ghost stories often use the atmospheric and narrative tropes of gothic literature. But a story with a ghost is not inherently gothic. Gothic fiction draws its horror from systems. White southern gothic literature is focused on the guilt and horror of upheld legacies of slavery. Black southern gothic is focused on the terror and pain of experienced legacies of slavery. Romantic and Victorian gothic literature is focused on familial trauma and the existential terror accompanying industrialization. The haunting of any gothic narrative is inherently collective. It is not about one person or artifact.

On the face of it, an hacienda is a great setting for a gothic novel. But because this book repeatedly rejects the collective legacy of the hacienda in favor of focusing on a few evil individuals, the potential horror and dread of the setting is reduced to tawdry questions of logistics: how can we banish the ghost if we can't find her body? How can my silks be covered in blood but then fine? etc.

The book does gesture at a true gothic aesthetic on occasion. We are repeatedly told, for example, that the Solórzanos' legacy is poison to the hacienda. But that's all it is, telling. We don't feel it. We don't internalize it. The sense of dread is explicitly coupled to Doña Catalina's presence, and when she is gone, so is our terror.

Given a hideous bitch and her rapist husband, you can construct a very terrifying ghost story. You could easily write a horror novel with these two people. However, if you want to write a gothic story, you need to understand and commit to the genre. The book ends with Andrés luxuriating in the big, fancy, blameless house built and still owned by his family's oppressors. This is antithetical to gothic literature. It simply does not work.
